title: Regional affinity, hysteresis, and probabilistic failover — design notes
body:
Summary:

These notes capture a proposed design for multi-region traffic steering that prioritizes regional affinity for lower latency and data locality while avoiding global synchronized failovers and flip-flop during transient outages. The approach combines:

- preference-weighted routing (GeoDNS / control-plane weights)
- Anycast for coarse-grained region selection where applicable
- edge-local health + capacity signals
- hysteresis windows and a probabilistic failover mechanism to smooth transitions
- capacity-aware admission control to avoid overloading healthy regions during spillover

Goals:
- Preserve regional affinity for the majority of sessions to minimize p95 latency and cross-region egress.
- Fail fast for unhealthy regions but avoid global traffic avalanches if a single region reports transient issues.
- Support predictable canary and incremental rollouts across regions.
- Integrate with our control plane (config push + xDS-style) and metrics pipelines.

Constraints / assumptions:
- We operate in 6 active regions with regional Dedicated pools (us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1, etc.).
- Data-plane agents publish local health/capacity to the control plane every 5s.
- DNS is managed by a multi-provider stack supporting GeoDNS and EDNS-client-subnet annotations; Anycast is used for some low-latency endpoints.
- Some customers require strict regional residency (cannot cross region) — those requests must be honored prior to preference logic.

High-level design decisions:

1) Control-plane vs DNS vs Anycast responsibilities
- Use Anycast + local LB for first-hop connection locality where low-ttl DNS is not acceptable (e.g., streaming websocket endpoints). Anycast gives quick routing to closest POP.
- Use GeoDNS for long-lived HTTP clients where we can leverage small TTLs and preference weights. GeoDNS will be the canonical place for region preference weights, but it is a read-only reflection of decisions made in the control plane.
- The control plane computes region weights per route based on: regional latency SLOs, capacity headroom, recent error rates, customer residency flags, and business-tier preferences.

2) Affinity model
- Default: soft affinity for 90% of new requests — try to route to the preferred region. If the preferred region lacks headroom, route to the next-preferred region.
- Strong affinity (session stickiness) when a session_id or conversation_id is present: prefer the same region for the life of the session unless region becomes unhealthy for > hysteresis window.
- Affinity enforcement is token-aware. Route decisions use a consistent-hash on session_id + bucketed weights to keep distribution stable.

3) Hysteresis & stabilization
- For any region state change (healthy -> degraded or vice-versa) we apply a stabilization window to prevent flip-flop:
  - degrade_threshold: sustained error rate above 3% or p95 latency > 2x baseline for 30s -> mark degraded (soft).
  - unhealthy_threshold: sustained error rate above 7% or p95 latency > 3x baseline for 90s -> mark unhealthy (hard).
  - recovery_threshold: metrics under degrade_threshold for 120s -> mark healthy.
- During a degrade->healthy transition we use a ramp-up profile (25% -> 50% -> 100%) over 5 minutes to rehydrate traffic.

4) Probabilistic failover to avoid traffic avalanches
- When spilling traffic from region A to other regions, we do not immediately move 100% of the failing region’s traffic. Instead we use weighted probabilistic spillover:
  - Compute candidate destinations (B, C, …) with available capacity.
  - For each new request destined for A, if A is degraded/unhealthy, draw a random number r in [0,1]. If r < p_spill(A), route to backup region according to weight distribution; else attempt A.
  - p_spill starts small (0.05) when degrade first detected and grows exponentially toward 0.9 over a configured ramp (e.g., 5 minutes) if error signals persist.
- Rationale: randomized routing prevents synchronized retries from overwhelming a single backup region and spreads load probabilistically across multiple healthy regions.

5) Capacity-aware admission and per-region headroom
- Control plane maintains per-region capacity estimate (tokens/sec and active sessions). Backups must be chosen such that (current_load + expected_spill) <= safe_capacity (e.g., 75% of provisioned).
- If all candidates lack headroom, circuit-break to a lower-cost fallback model or return a controlled degraded response (503 with Retry-After and hint). For customers with strict residency, return 451 / policy error.

6) Data-plane implementation notes
- Each edge POP runs a local steering agent that:
  - pulls control-plane routing profiles (weights, ttl, thresholds) via authenticated gRPC stream.
  - exposes local health metrics aggregated from local workers.
  - runs routing decision logic locally for sub-10ms decision latency.
- Agents must be stateless regarding global decisions; they only persist short-lived session-affinity caches (LRU, TTL=24h).
- For anycast endpoints, we only permit intra-region rebalancing: if POP health degrades, BGP withdraw + control-plane weight updates used. Anycast cannot easily guarantee per-customer residency — for residency contracts we disable Anycast and use GeoDNS+sticky config.

7) DNS TTL and caching strategy
- GeoDNS records: TTL 20s for high-change routes (canary or unstable), 60s for normal preference routes, 300s for locked enterprise-only records.
- Publish DNS hints that indicate region preferences (EDNS options) for recursive resolvers; when possible, use short TTLs combined with control-plane push to edge agents to make data-plane authoritative.

8) Canary and rollout support
- Rollouts are modeled as incremental changes to region weights with explicit ramp schedules encoded in the control plane.
- Canary example: route 5% new sessions to eu-west1 for 10 minutes, monitor p95 and error rate. If metrics OK, increment to 20%, etc. Canary is enforced via probabilistic assignment at the edge agent.

9) Observability & alarms
- Key signals: regional p50/p95 latency, error_rate (4xx/5xx), CPU/GPU utilization by model, active sessions, queue depth, token throughput.
- Derived signals: regional_headroom_pct, spill_rate, routing_entropy (to detect hotspots), cross-region_egress_bytes.
- Alerts:
  - P1: region_unhealthy (unhealthy_threshold exceeded) -> page on-call SRE + ops.
  - P2: spill_rate sustained > 5% for 10m -> Slack channel and duty engineer.
  - P3: routing_entropy drops suddenly -> investigate possible misconfiguration or traffic storm.

10) Operational playbook (simplified)
- Automatic: control plane detects unhealthy region -> begins probabilistic spill over -> edge agents apply rate checks and route.
- Engineer flow: verify metrics, if targeted fix available (e.g., scaling) then prefer scaling; otherwise manually adjust weights.
- Emergency: if region is fully down, escalate to manual DNS/Anycast withdraw, then route via baseline global pool.
- Recovery: once metrics stabilize, ramp down p_spill and reintroduce traffic according to ramp-up profile.

11) Failure modes and mitigations
- Synchronized client retries: mitigate with jittered retry guidance in SDKs; probabilistic routing reduces correlated retries.
- DNS resolver caching longer than TTL: use control-plane hints, and for critical customers use IP pinning/enterprise overrides.
- Capacity estimation drift: conservative headroom defaults and periodic calibration tests (synthetic traffic).

12) Testing plan
- Chaos tests: region failure (simulate partial network partition), rapid flapping, heavy burst that forces spillover. Run against staging with scaled-down realistic traffic for 6 regions.
- Load tests: ramp global QPS and validate headroom calculations and backpressure.
- Canary paths: opt-in internal customers to validate behaviour before wider rollout.

Open questions / next steps:
- How do we differentiate spill policies for streaming websocket sessions vs short HTTP calls? (Proposed: prefer local Anycast for websockets; fallback via sticky session proxy if re-route required.)
- Integration with pricing tier: should premium customers be prioritized for spill targets? (Tie to contractual SLOs and SLA-engineered weights.)
- Policy UI on Console: expose per-customer residency enforcement and manual override knobs for SRE.

Action items:
- (Daniel) Prototype probabilistic spill algorithm in redwood-routing (PR referenced above) — 2 weeks.
- (Leila) Add synthetic calibration job for regional headroom metrics — 1 week.
- (Marco) Draft console UI wireframe for residency toggles and manual weight override — 2 weeks.
- (Priya) Create chaos test plan and schedule first run in staging — 2 weeks.

References:
- Confluence: PLAT-MULTI-REGION-ARCH-122
- Jira: PLAT-2401
- GitHub PR: repo/redwood-routing/pull/387

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on immediate traffic movement and emphasizes smoothing. Looking for feedback on thresholds, p_spill ramp shape (linear vs exponential), and whether to centralize probabilistic decision in control plane vs local agent.

End of doc.
